evidenceAudit.scope: Adults with acute pancreatitis in the emergency department and first week of admission. Verified against the WSES 2019 severe acute pancreatitis guideline, NICE NG104 and the Saudi MOH Intra-abdominal Infections Treatment Protocol (antibiotic indications).
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 12 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: Fluid volumes and analgesic doses — local protocol
ACG 2024 guideline not reviewed (not open access)

pathophysiology.summary: Acute pancreatitis is acute inflammation of the pancreas with acinar cell destruction. Premature activation of digestive enzymes injures the gland and triggers a systemic inflammatory response (SIRS) that can progress to organ failure; severity is defined by organ failure lasting more than 48 h and by local complications such as necrosis.
keyMechanisms: Common causes: gallstones and alcohol; others include hypertriglyceridaemia (above 11.3 mmol/L), hypercalcaemia, drugs, microlithiasis, hereditary and autoimmune pancreatitis, tumours and pancreas divisum (NICE, WSES).
SIRS causes capillary leak and third-space fluid loss → hypovolaemia, haemoconcentration (rising haematocrit), rising urea and AKI; early resuscitation aims to protect pancreatic microcirculation.
Organ failure (respiratory, cardiovascular, renal) persisting more than 48 h defines severe disease; about 1 in 3 such patients die (WSES).
(Peri)pancreatic necrosis develops over days; it is best seen on contrast CT after 72 h. Infection of necrosis peaks in weeks 2–4.
Intra-abdominal hypertension and abdominal compartment syndrome can complicate severe disease.

symptoms: Sudden severe epigastric pain, often radiating to the back.
History of gallstones or heavy alcohol intake (but do not assume alcohol is the cause just because the patient drinks — NICE).
physicalSigns: Signs of hypovolaemia; jaundice suggests biliary obstruction or cholangitis.
Tachypnoea, hypoxaemia, pleural effusion; altered mental status; oliguria (organ failure).
redFlags: Organ failure (hypotension, hypoxaemia, AKI) — especially persisting despite fluids → ICU
SIRS on admission (risk of progression to organ failure)
Cholangitis (fever, jaundice, deranged LFTs) → ERCP indicated

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Free air; CT if the diagnosis is uncertain.
High lactate, pain out of proportion; CT.
Right upper quadrant pain, ultrasound findings; may coexist.
ECG and troponin in epigastric pain.
Kidney disease, appendicitis, cholecystitis, bowel obstruction (WSES).

ruleIn.expectedFinding: More than 3 times the upper limit of normal.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Lipase is preferred (more sensitive, longer window: rises 4–8 h, peaks 24 h, elevated 8–14 days). Amylase rises 6–24 h and normalises within 3–7 days. Level does not predict severity.
ruleIn.normalValue: Below the laboratory upper limit of normal

clinicalManagement.title: Confirm the diagnosis and look for the cause
actions: Diagnosis needs 2 of 3: typical pain; lipase/amylase more than 3× ULN; characteristic imaging.
Ultrasound on admission for gallstones; LFTs; triglycerides and calcium if not biliary or alcohol.
Assess for SIRS and organ failure; calculate BISAP.

clinicalManagement.title: Early goal-directed fluid resuscitation
actions: Start isotonic crystalloids early without waiting for haemodynamic worsening (Ringer's lactate may be preferred; evidence over saline is weak).
Reassess frequently (HR, BP, urine output, haematocrit, urea, creatinine, lactate) — avoid fluid overload.
WSES gives no fixed volume; adjust to age, weight, cardiac and renal function.

clinicalManagement.title: Analgesia
actions: Adequate analgesia for all within 24 h; no evidence for restricting opioids.
Avoid NSAIDs if AKI. Multimodal approach; PCA; epidural in severe cases needing prolonged high-dose opioids.

clinicalManagement.title: Feed early — do not starve
actions: Do not make nil by mouth unless there is a clear reason such as vomiting (NICE).
Moderately severe or severe: enteral nutrition started within 72 h (gastric or jejunal); parenteral only if enteral fails or is contraindicated.

clinicalManagement.title: Antibiotics only for infection
actions: Suspected infected necrosis (deterioration, gas in collection, raised procalcitonin): antibiotics that penetrate necrosis covering Gram-negative, Gram-positive and anaerobes — e.g. piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 h (MOH Table 2 severe regimen); carbapenem only in the very critically ill; quinolones only for beta-lactam allergy.

clinicalManagement.title: Gallstone pancreatitis
actions: Cholangitis → ERCP. CBD obstruction → ERCP. No ERCP for predicted severe biliary pancreatitis without cholangitis or obstruction.
Mild gallstone pancreatitis: laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the same admission.

clinicalManagement.title: Organ failure and complications
actions: Organ dysfunction: HDU monitoring; persistent organ failure despite fluids → ICU.
Monitor for intra-abdominal hypertension; limit excess fluids and sedation.

Necrotic, infective, haemorrhagic or systemic complications: seek advice from a specialist pancreatic centre (NICE); endoscopic (or percutaneous) step-up approach for infected necrosis, delaying intervention where possible.
No specific drug therapy beyond organ support and nutrition (WSES).

keyPoints: Diagnose with 2 of 3: pain, lipase over 3× ULN, imaging.
Early crystalloids with frequent reassessment; avoid overload.
Organ failure over 48 h = severe → ICU; CT at 72–96 h, not on day 1.
pitfalls: CT on admission when the diagnosis is clear.
Keeping patients nil by mouth without reason.

patientEducation: Cholecystectomy prevents recurrence in gallstone pancreatitis.
Severe disease: long recovery; possible diabetes or enzyme insufficiency later.
lifestyleAndDiet: Not applicable in the acute phase.
mdtReferrals: Gastroenterology/endoscopy for ERCP; general surgery for cholecystectomy.
ICU for persistent organ failure; specialist pancreatic centre for complications.
dischargeCriteria: Pain controlled on oral analgesia, eating, no organ failure.
Cause identified and addressed (cholecystectomy done or planned; alcohol advice).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Stop alcohol if alcohol-related; cholecystectomy on index admission for mild biliary pancreatitis; investigate idiopathic cases (repeat ultrasound, MRCP/EUS). Severe disease: recovery may take at least 3 times as long as the hospital stay (NICE).

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Typical abdominal pain; lipase or amylase more than 3× ULN; characteristic imaging
No organ failure; no local or systemic complications
Transient organ failure (under 48 h) and/or local or systemic complications without persistent organ failure
Persistent organ failure (over 48 h), single or multiple
Persistent organ failure AND infected (peri)pancreatic necrosis

regimens.duration: Guided by source control and cultures
adjustments: Critically ill: meropenem 1 g IV q8h (MOH); beta-lactam allergy: quinolone + metronidazole

medicationPlan.note: No antibiotics for sterile pancreatitis. Analgesic and fluid volumes are not specified by WSES or NICE — use local protocols. Check SFDA registration and hospital formulary.
